title: Conductors and insulators
summary: Explains how atomic structure makes materials conductors, insulators or semiconductors, how current flows, common cable types, and how temperature changes resistance.

sections.heading: Atomic structure
paragraphs: In an atom, negatively charged electrons orbit the positively charged nucleus. The orbits are known as shells, and the electrons in the outer shell are called valence electrons.
The number of valence electrons decides whether an element is a conductor or an insulator. Copper is a common conductor because it has just one valence electron, which is loosely attached.
bullets: Electron orbits are known as shells
Outer-shell electrons are valence electrons
More than 4 valence electrons: generally very stable, so the element is an insulator
Insulators have few free electrons in the outer shell; conductors have lots
Copper atom: 29 protons and 29 electrons

sections.heading: Examples of insulators and conductors
paragraphs: Insulators have few free electrons in their outer shell, while conductors have lots of them.
bullets: Insulators: mica, glass, ceramic, pure water, dry air, polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
Conductors: copper, silver, aluminium, gold, carbon, acid, alkaline or salt solutions

sections.heading: Electron flow and current flow
paragraphs: In any conductor there is constant random free electron movement as valence electrons break free from their atoms. If the material is connected across a battery, these free electrons are forced to move away from the negative plate, through the material, towards the positive plate.
bullets: Electron flow is from negative to positive
Conventional current flow is said to be from positive to negative

sections.heading: Cable types
paragraphs: Different cables use different insulation and conductor materials to suit their use. Some are fire resistant, some can be buried, and one (fibre optic) does not conduct electricity at all.
bullets: PVC single core thermoplastic: PVC/copper, used in conduit and trunking; needs containment unless used as protective conductor
Multicore PVC (twin/three-core and CPC): PVC insulation and PVC sheath, also XLPE/copper conductor; domestic and commercial with mechanical protection; XLPE insulated has higher current rating
Mineral insulated: magnesium oxide/copper with PVC oversheath; fire alarms, petrol filling stations; fire-resistant cable
Thermosetting fire retardant cables: silicone rubber/tinned copper aluminium screen; fire alarms; examples Fireforce, FP200 Firetuf
Steel wire armoured (SWA): PVC or XLPE/copper with steel armour; underground, industrial, commercial, agricultural; can be installed directly underground
CY, SY flex: C = copper braid, S = steel braid, Y = PVC; control cables and fixed installations/flex; indoors and outdoors
Data cables: PVC sheath/copper conductor, CAT 5e/CAT 6e UTP, HDPE insulation; internal use only
Fibre optic: glass fibres, LSOH; television, telephone and computer data; not an electrical conducting cable, transmits data by light wave

sections.heading: Semiconductors
paragraphs: Some elements are normally insulators but will conduct electricity at normal room temperatures if other elements are added to their molecular structure. These materials are known as semiconductors.
bullets: Common semiconductors: silicon and germanium
Both have 4 valence electrons

sections.heading: Effects of temperature on resistance
paragraphs: For most materials, resistance increases as temperature increases (not necessarily in the same proportion). This variable is the temperature coefficient of resistance, symbol α (alpha).

Copper has a positive temperature coefficient, which causes problems in installations and must be considered at the design stage. A cable carrying 10 A with a resistance of 1.1 Ω at 20°C gives an 11 V voltage drop; if the ambient temperature rises, the resistance and voltage drop increase, which may affect the equipment on that cable.
bullets: Positive temperature coefficient (PTC): resistance increases with temperature
Negative temperature coefficient (NTC): resistance decreases as temperature increases
Thermistors (PTC and NTC types) are used as temperature sensors
Semiconductors such as silicon have NTC characteristics
Copper coefficient at 0°C (R0): 0.0043 Ω/°C; at 20°C: 0.00396 Ω/°C

flashcards.back: It has just one valence electron, which is loosely attached.

Any four of: copper, silver, aluminium, gold, carbon, acid, alkaline or salt solutions.

flashcards.front: In which direction does electron flow go, compared with conventional current?
flashcards.back: Electron flow is negative to positive; conventional current flow is said to be positive to negative.

flashcards.front: What is mineral insulated cable used for?
flashcards.back: Fire alarms and petrol filling stations. It is magnesium oxide/copper with a PVC oversheath and is fire resistant.

flashcards.front: Where can steel wire armoured (SWA) cable be installed?
flashcards.back: Underground and in industrial, commercial and agricultural settings. It can be installed directly underground.

flashcards.front: Is fibre optic cable an electrical conductor?
flashcards.back: No. It transmits data by light wave through glass fibres.
An element that is normally an insulator but conducts at room temperature when other elements are added, e.g. silicon and germanium (4 valence electrons).

flashcards.front: What does the symbol α (alpha) stand for?
What is the difference between PTC and NTC?
flashcards.back: PTC: resistance rises as temperature rises. NTC: resistance falls as temperature rises.

flashcards.front: Why does a rise in ambient temperature affect cable voltage drop?
flashcards.back: Copper has a PTC, so cable resistance increases with temperature and the voltage drop increases.

quiz.q: What are the electrons in the outer shell of an atom called?
quiz.why: Electrons in the outer shell are known as valence electrons.

quiz.q: An atom has more than 4 valence electrons. What is the element generally?
options: A semiconductor only at high temperature
quiz.why: Any atom with more than 4 valence electrons is generally very stable, so the element is an insulator.

quiz.q: Why is copper a common electrical conductor?
options: It has no electrons in its outer shell
It has one loosely attached valence electron
quiz.why: Copper has just one valence electron, which is loosely attached.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an insulator?
quiz.why: Mica is listed as an insulator; carbon, silver and gold are conductors.

quiz.q: Which direction is conventional current flow said to be?
quiz.why: Conventional current flow is said to be positive to negative, while electron flow is negative to positive.

quiz.q: Which cable can be installed directly underground?
quiz.why: SWA cable with PVC or XLPE insulation and steel armour can be installed directly underground.

quiz.q: What is used as the insulation in mineral insulated cable?
quiz.why: Mineral insulated cable has magnesium oxide insulation with copper conductors and a PVC oversheath.

quiz.q: How does fibre optic cable transmit data?
quiz.why: Fibre optic is not an electrical conducting cable; it transmits data by light wave.

quiz.q: Which two materials are given as common semiconductors?
quiz.why: Silicon and germanium are common semiconductors, both with 4 valence electrons.

quiz.q: A cable carries 10 A and has a resistance of 1.1 Ω. What is the voltage drop?
quiz.why: Voltage drop = 10 A × 1.1 Ω = 11 V, and it rises if the cable warms up.

quiz.q: What happens to resistance in a material with a negative temperature coefficient when temperature increases?
quiz.why: With an NTC, an increase in temperature causes a decrease in resistance.
